structure.title: Concrete grievances
structure.text: The charter addresses inheritance, debt, royal demands, and administration through particular promises rather than a general theory of rights.

structure.title: Judgment and enforcement
structure.text: Clauses about legal process and observance seek to make those promises constrain royal conduct. Their scope must be read precisely.

people.name: Free men
people.text: A legal category narrower than the entire population.

context.title: A medieval settlement
context.text: The text responds to particular conflicts within a hierarchical society. Its later symbolic role is broader than its original distribution of protections.
context.takeaway: Do not silently replace medieval categories with universal rights.

context.title: Later afterlives
context.text: Subsequent readers used charter language to support new constitutional claims. Those uses matter, but are not all stated in this version.
context.takeaway: Separate original wording from later interpretation.

notice.why: Protection varies by status and circumstance.

notice.text: Follow the means of enforcing compliance.
notice.why: A promise limits power only if it can matter in practice.

opening: A king needs money and obedience. His barons have had enough of the way he obtains them. The settlement they force on John in 1215 attends to debts, inheritances, widows, courts, and the practical business of preventing royal power from swallowing other people's security. Among these particular grievances are promises that later generations would make much larger claims upon. Reading the charter reveals the narrow, contested beginnings of a powerful idea: even a ruler can be required to answer to rules he did not simply dictate.
